definitions.meaning: judges in British courts wear large horsehair wigs
very important people, the grand figures of an organisation

explanation.surface: A remark that judges count as very important people.
explanation.definitionFit: The slang term for important people comes from the large wigs once worn by men of rank, still worn by judges.

parts.note: means not a soldier on active service but one who serves an officer as a personal servant

explanation.definitionFit: An army officer's personal servant, himself a soldier, has this title.

parts.note: a wardrobe is a box for clothes, or gear, and a motorist has a box of gears

explanation.definitionFit: The car's transmission housing is a box holding its gears.

parts.note: recalls the proverb that a bird in the hand is worth two elsewhere, so birds there are worth half as much

explanation.definitionFit: The proverb says a bird in the hand is worth two in this place, so each one there is worth half.

clue.text: Can have a downward tendency in the main

definitions.text: Can have a downward tendency in the main

parts.words: Can have a downward tendency in the main
parts.note: 'in the main' seems to mean generally, but it means in the sea: something able to go down under water

explanation.definitionFit: A craft or device built to go under water is so described.

definitions.note: read as deer's kin: a relation of the deer

indicators.note: odd suggests the letters of junk mat are strange and out of order, signalling a rearrangement

explanation.surface: A strange mat made of junk sits among deer hides.
explanation.walkthrough: 'deerskin' looks like leather, but read it as 'deer's kin': the answer is a small Asian deer, a relative of the deer family.
explanation.definitionFit: The muntjak is a small barking deer of Asia, so it belongs to the deer family.

clue.text: But not the author of The Egoist

definitions.text: But not the author of The Egoist

parts.words: But not the author of The Egoist
parts.note: an egoist always talks of 'me', and Arthur of that surname was an author, though Meredith wrote the novel named

explanation.walkthrough: Arthur Mee wrote the Children's Encyclopaedia; his name sounds like the egoist's favourite word, yet George Meredith wrote The Egoist.
explanation.definitionFit: Arthur Mee, the British children's writer, is an author who shares his name with the self-centred pronoun.

clue.text: New York needs half our capital for this product

indicators.note: half tells you to keep only part of the city, dropping three of its six letters

parts.note: for a British paper, our capital is London

explanation.surface: A trade deal in which an American city and London share a product.
explanation.definitionFit: The synthetic fibre is a manufactured material, a factory-made thing.

parts.note: suggests a gangster or Oxford don, but Don Juan's sister would bear the feminine form of his name

explanation.definitionFit: The Spanish feminine diminutive of Juan would suit a sister of Don Juan.

clue.text: Clement and Heather are getting warm

parts.note: clement means mild and merciful, that is kind
ling is another name for heather

explanation.surface: Two friends named Clement and Heather warming up together.
explanation.walkthrough: Clement and Heather read as people's names but are the words clement (mild) and heather (the plant).
explanation.definitionFit: Setting a fire alight makes it start to burn and heat up.

clue.text: Religious paperback, well written, and easy to handle

parts.note: a tract is a short religious pamphlet, a cheap paper booklet
something well written is competently, ably done: able

explanation.surface: A religious pamphlet praised for its clear prose and handiness.
explanation.definitionFit: A tractable person or thing is docile and manageable, readily controlled.

clue.text: There's money to be made if you acquire the know-how

parts.note: L, for libra, is the old abbreviation for pounds sterling
money made is money earned, so to make money is to earn

explanation.surface: Advice that learning a skill pays off financially.
explanation.definitionFit: To learn is to gain knowledge or skill through study or practice.

parts.note: reads as a relaxed district but describes a leisurely walking pace, and also names a small town on the Northumberland coast

explanation.definitionFit: To stroll at an unhurried pace is the easy-going way to move, and the word is also a Northumbrian town's name.

parts.note: describes the scented oil distilled from plants, used in perfumery for its smell

explanation.definitionFit: A plant's distilled aromatic oil is called by this name because it carries the plant's essence, its scent.

clue.text: Tortoises maybe, that taught us by easy stages ?

definitions.text: Tortoises maybe, that taught us by easy stages ?

parts.words: Tortoises maybe, that taught us by easy stages ?
parts.note: laggards like tortoises, but also tutors who taught gradually, and stagecoaches travelling in easy stages

explanation.definitionFit: Dawdlers are so called, and the phrase also suggests unhurried tutors or old horse-drawn vehicles.

parts.note: suggests something from the Australian bush, but means a special railway service running out to a destination and back

explanation.definitionFit: A day trip by rail on a specially laid-on service, outward and return, is this kind of train.

clue.text: A treasure for those at a loss for a word

definitions.text: A treasure for those at a loss for a word

parts.words: A treasure for those at a loss for a word
parts.note: the Greek source of the word means treasure-house, and it is a book of synonyms

explanation.definitionFit: Roget's book of synonyms takes its title from a Greek word for a treasury, and helps a writer find words.

parts.note: arm means weapon, and a Highland dagger is worn tucked into the stocking beside the leg

explanation.definitionFit: The small Scottish knife worn in the sock with Highland dress is a weapon carried at the leg.

clue.text: Does he favour a surcingle? Sound idea

definitions.text: Does he favour a surcingle? Sound idea

parts.words: Does he favour a surcingle? Sound idea
parts.note: a surcingle is a horse's girth strap, but said aloud the word sounds like 'sir single': a knighted man who is unmarried

explanation.walkthrough: 'Sound idea' tells you to hear 'surcingle' as 'Sir Single': Sir for the knight, single for the bachelor. A surcingle is also a strap round a horse, apt for a knight.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the lowest rank of British knighthood, held by a knight belonging to no order.

clue.text: Cuts off in a zigzag way, being all battered

definitions.text: Cuts off in a zigzag way
definitions.meaning: to cut a document's edge in a toothed line, as with the old indenture deeds
read as two words, a battered thing is covered with dents

explanation.surface: A ragged cut on something bashed about.
explanation.definitionFit: Contracts were once cut along a jagged line, and a battered car is in dents, so the word works both ways.

clue.text: With a negative I nip round back — it's a view

indicators.note: back tells you to read the whole string of pieces from the end to the start

parts.note: no is a negative reply
O is round in shape

explanation.surface: A small dog's nip seen from behind, as somebody's point of view.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'nip' looks like a bite or pinch; here it is just letters, and 'back' turns the whole run of pieces end to start rather than only the last.
explanation.definitionFit: A personal belief or judgement on a matter is a viewpoint.

parts.note: an unknown woman in disguise in the Forest of Arden, the setting of As You Like It

explanation.definitionFit: In As You Like It, Celia hides her identity in the Forest of Arden under this assumed name.

parts.note: suggests rock music celebrities, but refers to the princess of Greek myth chained to a rock, later placed among the stars as a constellation

explanation.definitionFit: The Ethiopian princess chained to a sea rock and rescued by Perseus gave her name to a constellation and galaxy.

parts.note: in Gulliver's Travels the Lilliputians quarrel over which end of an egg to break, so the shape is egg-like

explanation.definitionFit: The word means egg-shaped, and Swift's Lilliputians went to war over how to crack eggs.

parts.note: looks like a stormy temperament, but means the sprite who serves Prospero in Shakespeare's play The Tempest

explanation.definitionFit: Prospero's airy servant in The Tempest raises the storm of the play's opening.

parts.note: a din is a loud, confused noise
when a noise abates it goes away, so the abatement is the go

explanation.surface: A campaign to reduce dogs barking.
explanation.definitionFit: The wild dog of Australia is a member of the canine family.

indicators.note: the word stands for the answer itself, which tells you to set the letters of white rose out in a different way

explanation.surface: Pointing to a white rose in a garden.
explanation.walkthrough: 'This' stands in for the answer: put the answer before 'white rose' and it tells you to arrange those letters in another way, and that rearrangement spells the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means in a different way, which is exactly what the anagram does to the flower's letters.

clue.text: " The music-hall singer attends a series Of Masses and fugues and" (Gilbert)

definitions.text: The music-hall singer attends a series Of Masses and fugues and

parts.words: The music-hall singer attends a series Of Masses and fugues and
parts.note: a line from Gilbert's lyric in The Mikado, whose next word, a slangy short form of opuses, completes the rhyme

explanation.definitionFit: Gilbert's slangy plural of opus, musical works, ends this line of the Mikado's list song.

clue.text: Arise, gamesmen all ! Get this with the opposition !

parts.note: to arise is to get up
all the players in games together form the sides

explanation.surface: A rallying cry to the players to rise and take on their opponents.
explanation.walkthrough: To 'get upsides with' someone is a British idiom for getting even with them.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom to get level with a rival uses this word, so it fills the gap in the defining phrase.

clue.text: Beautiful and bookish, but she's not for the Canon!

definitions.text: Beautiful and bookish, but she's not for the Canon!

parts.words: Beautiful and bookish, but she's not for the Canon!
parts.note: describes the lovely heroine of a book of the Apocrypha, a book left out of the accepted canon of scripture, and so not for a churchman to read in church

explanation.definitionFit: The virtuous beauty spied on by the elders appears in a book of the Apocrypha, excluded from the Protestant biblical canon.
